Chapter 6: Nutrition in Plants (class notes)

6.1 What is photosynthesis?
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. The plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny pores called stomata and absorbs water from the soil through its roots. Using the energy of sunlight, the plant combines carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose, a simple sugar, which it uses as food. The word equation is: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. Glucose that is not used at once is stored as starch.

6.2 Chlorophyll and chloroplasts
The green colour of leaves comes from a pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is found inside small structures in the leaf cells called chloroplasts. Chlorophyll traps light energy from the sun, which is why photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves. Leaves are broad and flat so that they can capture as much light as possible. Plants without chlorophyll, such as fungi, cannot photosynthesise and must obtain food in other ways.

6.3 Oxygen, the by-product
During photosynthesis oxygen is released as a by-product. The oxygen leaves the plant through the stomata and enters the air. This is the source of the oxygen that animals and humans breathe. A simple experiment with a water plant such as Hydrilla shows bubbles of oxygen gas being given off when the plant is kept in sunlight. The gas collected in the test tube relights a glowing splint, which proves that it is oxygen.

6.4 Why plants need water
Water is one of the raw materials of photosynthesis, so a plant cannot make food without it. Water also carries dissolved mineral salts such as nitrates from the soil up to the leaves. Water keeps the plant cells firm, or turgid, which keeps the stem upright and the leaves spread out; a plant short of water wilts. Finally, water that evaporates from the leaves in transpiration cools the plant on hot days.

6.5 Stomata and gas exchange
Stomata are tiny openings on the surface of leaves, mostly on the lower side. Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells that open and close it. Through the stomata the leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen and water vapour. Stomata usually open in daylight and close at night to reduce water loss.

6.6 Conditions needed for photosynthesis
Photosynthesis needs four things: sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water. The rate of photosynthesis increases with more light and more carbon dioxide up to a limit, and it is also affected by temperature. A variegated leaf, which has white patches without chlorophyll, tested with iodine shows starch only in the green parts, proving that chlorophyll is needed.

6.7 Other modes of nutrition
Some plants cannot make their own food. Cuscuta (dodder) is a parasite that takes ready-made food from the host plant it climbs on. The pitcher plant is insectivorous: insects trapped in its pitcher are digested to supply nitrogen. Fungi such as mushrooms are saprotrophs that feed on dead and decaying matter. Lichens are a partnership between an alga, which photosynthesises, and a fungus, which provides shelter and water.
